summary: In Greek mythology, Ligdus is a poor but honest Cretan of Phaestus (near Cnossus), husband of Telethusa and father of Iphis. In Ovid's Metamorphoses he vows to expose a daughter for want of a dowry; Isis prompts Telethusa to raise the child as a boy until the goddess transforms Iphis into a man to marry Ianthe. Distinct from other figures only loosely tied to the Iphis catalogue.
etymology: Latin Ligdus (Ovid); Greek form uncertain in the surviving tale.

sections.heading: The vow at Phaestus
paragraphs: Ovid sets Ligdus near Phaestus and Cnossus: when Telethusa is with child he swears to kill the infant if it is a girl, because they cannot afford a dowry. Isis appears to Telethusa in a dream and bids her disregard the vow and raise the child whatever its sex.
A daughter is born; Telethusa names the child Iphis — a name usable for either sex — and raises her as a boy. Ligdus remains unaware until the wedding crisis forces the goddess's intervention.

sections.heading: Father of Iphis
paragraphs: When Iphis is betrothed to Ianthe, daughter of Telestes, Telethusa and Iphis pray at Isis' shrine; the goddess transforms Iphis into a youth so the marriage can proceed. Ligdus' role is the social pressure — poverty and the exposure vow — that drives the metamorphosis plot.
The atlas id ligdus-crete is this Ovidian Cretan father alone. Other Iphis figures (Patroclus' captive, Thespiad mother, Argive king) belong to other nodes.
